This study used qualitative methods (phenomenological-hermeneutic approach with narrative analysis of patient interviews) to explore patients' experiences and perceptions of cardiac tele-rehabilitation, specifically addressing how they adapt to life with heart disease in a home-based telerehabilitation program. It directly examines stakeholders' (patients') experiences, perceptions, and behaviours about the provision of home-based telerehabilitation services.

This paper reports on scientific events of a WHO conference launching the Rehabilitation 2030 initiative. It does not use qualitative methods for data collection and analysis (it is a conference report), nor does it explore patients', caregivers', or healthcare providers' experiences, perceptions, or behaviours about the provision of home-based rehabilitation or telerehabilitation services.

This study employed qualitative methods (purposive sample, interviews, thematic analysis) to qualitatively describe upper extremity use at home, previous home exercise programs, and the acceptability of a novel home-based intervention (NeuroGame Therapy) for stroke survivors. It explores patients' experiences and perceptions of home-based rehabilitation services.

This qualitative study (semi-structured interviews, thematic analysis) investigated stroke patients' experiences and expectations during their transition from hospital to home after participating in the STRENGTH program, which includes a home-based component. It explores patients' perceptions of therapy received in both hospital and home settings, addressing their experiences with home-based rehabilitation provisions.

The provided abstract describes the Growing Up in Australia Child Health CheckPoint study (population phenotypes, biosamples), which is unrelated to home-based rehabilitation for heart failure. There is no indication that this study used qualitative methods to explore stakeholders' experiences, perceptions, or behaviours about home-based rehabilitation provision.

This study used a qualitative phenomenological approach (Colaizzi’s method) to explore the lived experiences of burn survivors after a 6-month period of home care following hospital discharge. It directly examines patients' experiences and perceptions of home-based rehabilitation (home care) services.

This qualitative study (semi-structured interviews, content analysis) identified reasons for the provision of informal rehabilitation services at home to stroke relatives by Thai caregivers. It explores caregivers' perceptions, experiences, and behaviours regarding home-based rehabilitation provision.

This qualitative study (semi-structured interviews, thematic analysis) explored orthopaedic healthcare professionals' perceptions of opportunities and challenges of using wearable technology in rehabilitation, specifically noting its value for supporting patients at home. It examines healthcare providers' experiences and perceptions about a technology enabling home-based rehabilitation.

This study is a systematic review and meta-analysis focused on clinical effectiveness (SMD, MD, confidence intervals) of telerehabilitation for motor function recovery. It does not use qualitative methods for data collection and analysis, nor does it explore stakeholders' experiences, perceptions, or behaviours about telerehabilitation provision.

This qualitative secondary data analysis (rigorous content analysis) examined a nurse specialist's responses and advice in a web-based supportive intervention for stroke family caregivers. It explores caregivers' experiences, perceptions, and behaviours (seeking advice, support, information) regarding a home-based telerehabilitation/support service.

This qualitative case study (focus groups, phone interviews, video recordings, document analysis) examined how telerehabilitation becomes part of clinical routines, identifying factors enabling or constraining its integration. It explores experiences and perceptions of healthcare providers, managers, patients, and family members regarding telerehabilitation provision in rehabilitation settings.

This mixed methods study included qualitative components (semi-structured questionnaires, telephone interviews) to evaluate a digital version of a cardiac rehabilitation programme. It explored patients' and health professionals' perceptions of user-friendliness and effectiveness, addressing their experiences with a home-based digital rehabilitation programme.

This study used qualitative interviews and content analysis to investigate the experiences of ten patients who received video-based physiotherapy at home for two months after shoulder joint replacement. It directly explores patients' experiences and perceptions of home-based telerehabilitation provision.

This study evaluated an online cardiac rehabilitation program using both qualitative and quantitative methods. The qualitative evaluation (focus groups, interviews) explored patients' perceptions of the online CR approach as a useful instrument for self-management, addressing their experiences with home-based telerehabilitation provision.

This convergent parallel mixed-methods study used qualitative data (semi-structured interviews, document analysis) to analyze barriers and facilitators of implementing home-based cardiac rehabilitation (HBCR) programs. It explores stakeholders' experiences, perceptions, and behaviours regarding the provision of home-based rehabilitation services.

While this study used qualitative methods (semi-structured interviews), it focused on mobility-related preferences and outcomes following post-acute rehabilitation in inpatient or skilled nursing facilities, not on experiences, perceptions, or behaviours about the provision of home-based rehabilitation or telerehabilitation services.

This systematic review and meta-analysis focused on the effectiveness of physiotherapy with telerehabilitation on postoperative functional outcomes and quality of life. It does not use qualitative methods to explore stakeholders' experiences, perceptions, or behaviours about telerehabilitation provision.

This mixed methods study (postal survey, focus groups, think-aloud interviews) aimed to co-design a web-based rehabilitation program (ESCAPE-pain) that users find engaging and useful. It explored patients' opinions, experiences, and perceptions regarding a home-based telerehabilitation service, addressing their requirements for such provision.

This paper is a methodological introduction to the GRADE-CERQual approach for assessing confidence in qualitative evidence synthesis findings. It is not a primary study exploring stakeholders' experiences, perceptions, or behaviours about home-based rehabilitation or telerehabilitation provision.

This qualitative study (focus groups, phenomenological approach) explored perceptions about physical activity information delivery methods and messengers for people with spinal cord injury. It does not specifically address experiences, perceptions, or behaviours about the provision of home-based rehabilitation or telerehabilitation services.

This study conducted a literature search and review to classify aspects of home care programs for traumatic spinal cord injury. It does not use qualitative methods for data collection and analysis (it is a literature review), nor does it explore stakeholders' experiences, perceptions, or behaviours about home-based rehabilitation provision.

This is a protocol for a Cochrane Review (Qualitative), not a completed study. It proposes to identify barriers/facilitators to physical activity for people with bipolar disorder but has not collected or analyzed any data yet. It does not explore experiences, perceptions, or behaviours about home-based rehabilitation provision.

This qualitative study (interviews with patients and staff, thematic analysis) examined patients' experiences of being offered a choice between home-based and hospital-based cardiac rehabilitation. It explores patients' and healthcare providers' perceptions, experiences, and behaviours regarding the provision of home-based rehabilitation services.

This is an update of a Cochrane review focused on determining the effectiveness and cost of early discharge hospital at home versus inpatient care. It does not use qualitative methods for data collection and analysis, nor does it explore stakeholders' experiences, perceptions, or behaviours about home-based rehabilitation provision.

This qualitative case-oriented study (repeated interviews, grounded theory analysis) explored how older adults who received home-based rehabilitation perceived staff during a 6-month period. It directly explores patients' experiences and perceptions of staff interactions in home-based rehabilitation provision.

This sequential explanatory mixed-method study included qualitative data analysis (thematic analysis) to examine the usability of a mobile exercise app for people with physical disabilities. It explored users' experiences and perceptions of the app, including how it circumvented barriers to exercise associated with leaving the home, addressing their views on a technology supporting home-based rehabilitation/activity.

The abstract indicates this study aims to assess the effects of home-based multidimensional survivorship programmes on quality of life (an outcomes-focused evaluation). There is no clear indication that it used qualitative methods to explore stakeholders' experiences, perceptions, or behaviours about the provision of such programmes.

Despite an abstract mismatch (appearing to discuss neurocysticercosis), the title indicates this is an interview study about stroke patients' expectations regarding coming home with early supported discharge and home rehabilitation. As an interview study, it likely used qualitative methods to explore patients' experiences, perceptions, and expectations about home-based rehabilitation provision.

This qualitative study (thematic analysis) explored reasons for nonattendance and noncompletion in cardiac rehabilitation programmes, identifying personal, programme, and practical factors. It examined patients' perceptions of programme suitability, intensity, and purpose, which includes considerations relevant to home-based cardiac rehabilitation options.

This appears to be a book chapter or review providing an overview of telerehabilitation concepts, history, technology, and case studies. It is not a primary qualitative study exploring stakeholders' experiences, perceptions, or behaviours about telerehabilitation provision.

This systematic review compared outcomes (function, cognition, quality of life) of home-based versus inpatient rehabilitation using quantitative synthesis. It does not use qualitative methods for data collection and analysis, nor does it explore stakeholders' experiences, perceptions, or behaviours about home-based rehabilitation provision.
